lead: At Horizonte, the process changes when someone complains loudly: a scare created the check of every order, and nobody wrote down when or why. Software does not change like that. It has a version number, a record of each change, and a tested way to go back. In this lesson you treat the process the same way and record the move from version 1.0 to 2.0.
objetivo: record the process change v1 → v2 with the reason, evidence, approver, phased rollout, and the way back, the way it is done with software.

aprende.t: Give the process a version number
Turn a complaint into a proposal, not a change
Promote step by step, with approval from whoever is accountable
Write the trigger and the way back first

hero_alt: In a meeting room, a screen shows two colored block diagrams side by side, the one on the left longer; a woman holds a sheet with a checkbox and the team listens.

secoes.sub: From the version in use to the next one, with the way back written down. Click each step.
secoes.volta: It got worse or hit the trigger: go back to the previous version, which was kept

nos.detalhe: The process as it is today, with a number, a date, and an owner: the map from lesson 3 is v1.0. Without the version in use written down, there is nothing to compare and nowhere to go back to.

A change starts from an observed problem (with the source cases) and a hypothesis: "if we change X, indicator Y improves without worsening Z". An isolated complaint opens a proposal; it does not change the process by itself.
The new version runs first in the pilot scope, for an agreed period, and the lesson 6 indicators are compared with the baseline, over similar periods.

Promote, reject, or wait for more data. Whoever decides answers for the result and is not the one who proposed it: if the proposal comes from the process owner, whoever is above them decides. The decision is logged with the reason.

The promoted version goes into use, in phases. The previous one stays written down and labeled, with the step-by-step to bring it back. No worse version replaces the current one because a system decided so.

secoes.legenda: Rule 3 of the agentic process (AI Management area): promoting and rolling back are steps, not accidents. LOOP-R cycle and the change contract of the Gestoria method (INEMA).

secoes.sub: Four rules. Horizonte is a fictional study company; the dates and decisions in the example are fictional too.

texto: Give the process a number. A change that cuts, moves, or merges a step bumps the whole version (1.0 to 2.0). An adjustment that doesn't touch the steps, like changing the deadline for a reply, bumps the decimal (2.0 to 2.1).
Keep a one-line history per version: number, date, what changed, why, who approved. It's what answers, six months from now, why the process is the way it is.

exemplo.texto: The check of every order went in on 10/14 with no record. In the new history, it shows up as part of v1.0, with the reason Patrícia remembered: the improper discounts that week.

texto: One bad case is a signal, not evidence. It opens a proposal with the problem, the source cases, and the hypothesis. The change only goes in after it is tested and approved.
This protects the process from whoever complained loudest last, even when the one complaining is the owner.

exemplo.texto: A customer complained about an invoice that took three days. Instead of creating a new check, Patrícia opened a proposal: the source case is P3, and the hypothesis is to move the registration check to intake.

passos.titulo: Promote a little at a time
texto: The new version starts in the pilot scope, for a set period, with the indicators compared to the baseline. Only after that does it apply to all cases.
Promotion is a decision for whoever answers for the result, with the numbers on the table, and never for whoever proposed it. If the proposer is the process owner, whoever is above them decides.

exemplo.texto: Phase 1, two weeks: v2.0 only for registered customers with orders up to R$ 5 thousand. Phase 2: all orders. Patrícia, the process owner, proposes; Carlos approves each phase by looking at the three indicators.

texto: Before changing, write down when to go back (the trigger, with a number) and how to go back (the steps, who does them, how fast). Deciding this after the problem is deciding in a panic.
Rolling back is not failure: it's what lets you test without fear. What can't happen is the previous version having disappeared.

exemplo.texto: Go back to v1.0 if the billing returns stay above the baseline for two weeks in a row, or if an order goes out with a discount outside the policy. Patrícia decides within one business day; the spreadsheet and the paper come back the next day.

secoes.titulo: Templates to copy: change record and version history
secoes.sub: The record follows each change; the history has one line per version. The tabs show Horizonte.

Rule: cutting, moving, or merging a step = a whole new version; an adjustment that doesn't touch the steps = decimal.

You are a process auditor. Below is the record of a process change in my
company. Don't decide whether the change is good. Point out:

1. Whether the problem has source cases or is just an impression.
2. Whether the hypothesis says which indicator improves and which one can't get worse.
3. Whether the person who approves is different from the person who proposed.
4. Whether the rollback trigger has a number and a deadline, and whether the steps
   to go back say who does each one.
5. What would be missing for someone, six months from now, to understand this change.

Record:
"""<paste>"""

abas.html:
Change no. 001 · WhatsApp order → invoice · v1.0 → v2.0 · Horizonte, fictional study company

  • Problem: orders come back from billing because of incomplete registration and go through 4 handoffs (cases P1 to P5).
  • Hypothesis: by cutting the handoffs, checking only exceptions, and moving registration to intake, the time to invoice and the returns drop, with no discount outside the policy.
  • Proposed by: Patrícia · approves: Carlos.
  • Evidence: four-week baseline counted in the app and the ERP before the change; test in phase 1, for two weeks.
  • Phases: 1) registered customers with orders up to R$ 5k; 2) all orders.
  • Rollback: returns above the baseline for two weeks in a row, or one order with a discount outside the policy. Patrícia decides within one business day. Steps: Juliana goes back to copying into the spreadsheet and printing; Rafael turns off the automatic handoff to the ERP; finance goes back to typing it in. v1.0 is kept in the process folder.

VersionWhat changedStatus
1.0Mapped with 13 steps, including the check of every order, created on 10/14 after the improper discountskept
2.08 steps: 5 eliminated, check of exceptions and sample, registration at intakein testing (phase 1)
2.1Weekly sample from 10 to 15 orders during phase 2 (adjustment, steps untouched)proposed

Fictional study dates and decisions.

• A change with no number. If you can't say which version the process is on, you can't go back.
  • Whoever proposes doesn't approve. Approval comes from whoever answers for the result and didn't make the proposal; if the process owner proposed it, whoever is above them approves.
  • A vague trigger. "If it gets worse" is not a trigger; "returns above X for two weeks" is.
  • Previous version erased. Keep the v1.0 map, tagging sheet, and executor chart.
  • Changing everything at once. Phases let you see the effect before it applies to everyone.

secoes.sub: Horizonte's record is for practice; your process's record is for real.

exercicios.texto: Use the redesign sheet from lesson 4, the chart from lesson 5, and the indicator sheets from lesson 6. Fill in the change record and the history without looking at the tabs. Run the review prompt and fix what it points out.
exercicios.pronto: the record has a problem with source cases, a hypothesis with an indicator and a guardrail, an approver different from whoever proposed it, 2 phases with a scope, 2 rollback triggers with a number and a deadline, and the steps back with who does each one; the history has the 1.0 and 2.0 rows.

exercicios.texto: Make the change record from the current version of your process to the redesigned one, and the history. Agree with whoever approves it before you start phase 1.
exercicios.pronto: the record is complete, with the baseline from lesson 6 as starting evidence, the approver agreed in writing, the date for phase 1, and the current version saved somewhere another person can find it.

secoes.sub: 4 questions. The explanation appears after your attempt.

perguntas.p: An important customer complained about a delay. The owner wants to create a new check right away. What does a versioned process call for?
opcoes: Create the check today and record it later, if it works
Wait for three more identical complaints before touching anything
Open a proposal with the case and the hypothesis, and test first
perguntas.explica: A complaint is a signal, not evidence. It opens a proposal; the change goes in tested and approved. Creating it now and recording it later is changing on impulse; waiting for more complaints ignores a case that may point to a real problem.

perguntas.p: You changed the weekly sample size from 10 to 15 orders, without touching the steps. What version is it?
opcoes: 2.1: an adjustment that doesn't touch the steps bumps the decimal
3.0: every approved change bumps the whole version
None: only a change to a step needs a version
perguntas.explica: Cutting, moving, or merging a step bumps the whole number; an adjustment that doesn't touch the steps bumps the decimal. Even the adjustment goes into the history.

perguntas.p: When do you write the rollback trigger?
opcoes: Before the change, with a number, a deadline, and who decides
When the first problem shows up in phase 1
At the end of phase 1, looking at the indicators
perguntas.explica: A trigger decided after the problem, or after looking at the phase 1 result, is decided on impulse, and everyone pulls in a different direction. Written beforehand, the rollback is a planned step.

perguntas.p: Who approves promoting version 2.0 at Horizonte?
opcoes: Patrícia, who answers for the process and knows the numbers
Carlos, because whoever proposes doesn't approve their own change
Rafael, who will turn on the integration and knows what changes
perguntas.explica: Patrícia answers for the process, but she is the one who proposed v2.0: whoever is above her approves, looking at the indicators against the baseline. Whoever proposes presents the evidence; no version goes in by a system's decision.

itens.texto: Step changed, whole number; adjustment, decimal. One row per version.
Source case, hypothesis, test against the baseline.
Pilot scope first; whoever answers for it approves, never whoever proposed.
Trigger with a number, steps with names, previous version saved.
